title: The classroom at Nicopolis
hookLine: the Discourses are a student's notes of Epictetus teaching young men

cards: Northwest Greece, under the Roman emperors. A city by the sea with a name that means victory city. In a room somewhere in it, a teacher who was once enslaved is talking to a class of young men.
He teases them. He loses patience with them. He tells them stories about their own vanity until they squirm.
And in the room, a student is writing down every word he can catch. A new part of the path begins here.

teach.b: Epictetus was enslaved in Rome. Ancient writers name his owner: Epaphroditus, himself a freedman who had served Nero. Epictetus studied philosophy with the Stoic Musonius Rufus, and at some point was freed.
Then, the writer Aulus Gellius reports, the emperor Domitian expelled the philosophers from Rome, and Epictetus moved across the sea to Nicopolis.
In victory city he opened a school, and young men came to hear him. One of those students was Arrian, who later wrote a history of Alexander the Great.

teach.h: ARRIAN WROTE DOWN THE VERY WORDS.
teach.b: Arrian wrote down what he heard. In a short letter at the front of the Discourses, he says he didn't compose them like a book.

He tried to record his teacher's words as nearly as he could, in the very words used, as reminders of his thinking and his frankness. That's why they sound like speech, full of questions and jokes and rough corners.

teach.h: THE HANDBOOK SUMMARIZED; THIS IS THE ROOM.

teach.b: The Discourses are the classroom. You'll hear Epictetus interrupt, argue with imaginary students, mock the proud and lose patience with the lazy. It's the difference between reading a recipe and standing in the kitchen.
For the next weeks, this path stands in the kitchen.

how: Some readers of the Discourses read passages aloud, since Arrian says he tried to keep his teacher's spoken words rather than write a polished book.

practice: If you have a book nearby that matters to you, open it to one paragraph; if not, recall one section of the handbook you chose yesterday.
Read it or say it out loud, slowly, the way it might have sounded in a classroom by the sea, and notice what you hear that you missed reading silently. Then rest in the quiet after the words.

wordCard.voice: Arrian. The student who wrote down his teacher's words as nearly as he could, at the school in Nicopolis. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: victory city, from nikē, victory, and polis, city; Epictetus' home and school.
